scenes.narration: This slide compares three governance controls by the point at which they act. On the left, a preventive AWS Organizations SCP denies a disallowed API call before a resource can be changed, illustrated by protecting mandatory security logging. In the middle, a proactive Control Tower control validates a proposed CloudFormation resource against a supported requirement and can block provisioning of an invalid resource. On the right, a detective AWS Config rule evaluates a deployed resource and marks it noncompliant after the fact. That finding alone does not undo the change or automatically block it; remediation is another step. The bottom warning states that SCPs define the maximum allowed permissions but do not grant actions. It also reminds us that control support varies by Region and resource. Choose preventive enforcement when an action must never happen, proactive checks when a proposed configuration must be rejected, and detection when ongoing compliance visibility is needed.

scenes.narration: This architecture explains why an IAM Allow does not automatically mean an API request succeeds. Start with the AWS Organizations root in the middle. It has a FullAWSAccess SCP baseline. Beneath it, a production OU attaches another SCP explicitly denying the EC2 TerminateInstances action. On the right, a role in a production member account has an identity policy allowing EC2 start, stop and terminate actions. Follow those actions into the effective-permissions results. Starting and stopping an instance remain allowed if no other control blocks them. Terminating is denied because the production OU's explicit deny wins over the identity policy. The bottom compares deny-list and allow-list SCP strategies, and explains that allow-list designs need appropriate Allow permissions at every applicable hierarchy level. Notice the exceptions: the Organizations management account is not restricted by the organization's SCPs, service-linked roles are not restricted by SCPs, and the root user in a member account is affected. The exam rule is maximum permissions, never a grant.

scenes.narration: This diagram compares SCP and RCP controls and illustrates their different coverage. The left boxes show that an SCP limits the maximum actions of principals in member accounts. An RCP instead restricts access to supported resources belonging to member accounts, including relevant requests by principals from outside the organization. Look at the central example. An external principal requests S3 GetObject from a bucket in a member account. The bucket resource policy might allow that principal, but the RCP explicitly denies the request because the source is from an untrusted organization. Follow the red result: the request is blocked despite the bucket policy's Allow. On the right, RCPs can be attached at applicable hierarchy levels and inherited by supported resources. The notes highlight default broad-access baseline behavior, management-account exclusions and documented service principal exceptions. RCP support is service and action dependent, and an RCP cannot grant access by itself. Use SCPs to limit member-account identities and RCPs to protect supported member-account resources.
